desc:
You may choose any contiguous substring of s (of length 1 up to the whole string) and reverse it in place. Reversing a substring of length 1 changes nothing, so the original string is always one possible result.

Return the number of distinct strings that can be obtained with exactly one such reversal.

s = "aab"  ->  3   ("aab", "baa", "aba")
s = "abc"  ->  4   ("abc", "bac", "cba", "acb")
s = "aaaa" ->  1
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: There are about n2/2 substrings, and you cannot afford to build each result. Think about which reversals produce the same string.
Reversing [i, j] when s[i] == s[j] gives the same string as reversing the inner substring [i+1, j-1]. So only reversals whose two end characters differ can produce something new.

Show that two different reversals with s[i] != s[j] always give different strings (the first and last changed positions are exactly i and j). The answer is 1 + (number of pairs i < j with s[i] != s[j]).
editorial: Take a reversal of [i, j]. If s[i] == s[j], the outer two characters swap with themselves, so the result equals the reversal of [i+1, j-1]. Repeating this argument, such a reversal equals either the original string (inner range empty or of length 1) or a reversal whose end characters differ. So every reachable string is either s or the result of a reversal with s[i] != s[j].

Now take a reversal of [i, j] with s[i] != s[j]. Position i receives s[j] and position j receives s[i], so both change, while everything outside [i, j] is untouched. Hence the first and last positions where the result differs from s are exactly i and j, which means different pairs give different strings, and none of them equals s.

The answer is therefore 1 + #{(i, j): i < j, s[i] != s[j]} = 1 + C(n, 2) - ∑letters C(cnt, 2), computed from 26 letter counts in O(n) time and O(1) space. The maximum, about 1.8 billion for n = 60,000, still fits in a signed 32-bit integer.
